title: Knowledge Management in Law Firms
pub: Journal of Information, Law and Technology (JILT)
author: Stefane M. Kabene · Philip King · Nada Skaini

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess generative AI’s jagged capabilities directly, but materially extends the cluster’s operating-model argument. It shows that technology-enabled legal work depends on an integrated knowledge infrastructure, especially organisational structure, culture, incentives and systematic capture of lawyers’ tacit expertise; it also identifies hourly billing and scarce lawyer time as barriers to realising efficiency gains.
qs: Knowledge Infrastructure  A firm’s knowledge infrastructure capability is realised via technology, organizational structure, and culture.
However, if billing structures are not changed, the efficiencies obtained through KM may not benefit a firm financially (Kay, 2003, p.1).

kp.k: Knowledge management requires organizational change, not just technology
kp.d: This 2006 paper addresses knowledge management (KM), rather than AI, through analysis of existing literature. The authors argue that successful implementation depends jointly on technology, organizational structure, culture and human resources. Its claims about competitive advantage and sustainability are arguments and recommendations, rather than results from a newly reported law-firm experiment.
qs: The scope of this paper is to examine what human resource professionals can do, and describe how human resources management can play a critical role, in ensuring the successful implementation of knowledge management within law firms.
A firm’s knowledge infrastructure capability is realised via technology, organizational structure, and culture.

kp.k: Tacit expertise differentiates lawyers but resists codification
kp.d: Drawing on Kofoed and other literature, the authors distinguish explicit knowledge acquired through education from experience-based tacit knowledge. They identify sharing tacit expertise as a central law-firm challenge, while acknowledging that some organizational knowledge cannot be efficiently articulated or fully described.
qs: The sharing of tacit knowledge among lawyers is the single biggest knowledge related issue in a law firm.

A great deal of organizational knowledge remains tacit as it cannot be efficiently explained using formal language, and because it is unfeasible to describe all aspects necessary for success and performance (Madhavan, 1996, p.7).

kp.k: Knowledge processes encompass acquisition, conversion, application and protection
kp.d: The paper presents a framework in which infrastructure supports acquiring information, converting it into usable knowledge, applying it and protecting it from outsiders. Electronic repositories hold knowledge artefacts, but effective KM requires both infrastructure and processes rather than storage alone.
qs: An organization’s knowledge process capability consists of four elements: acquisition, conversion, application and protection.
Therefore, the success of a KM program depends on how competently a company develops and utilises both its knowledge infrastructure and its knowledge processing capabilities.

kp.k: Knowledge reuse reduces duplication and improves work allocation
kp.d: Reporting Dublin (2005), the authors describe lawyers duplicating research and drafting documents from scratch despite available models. They argue that KM can improve access to current information and best practices, help allocate work to appropriately experienced people, and avoid wasted time and poor-quality work.
qs: First of all, Dublin (2005) notes that research in a law firm is often duplicated by a number of lawyers meaning agreements, memoranda and other documents may be created from scratch when adequate models for such documents already exist.
Other consequences of such action include wasted time and poor quality work.

kp.k: Clients pressure firms toward technology-enabled efficiency
kp.d: Citing Becker and colleagues, Khandelwal and Gottschalk, and Dublin, the paper reports declining client loyalty, more value-conscious purchasing and pressure to achieve productivity gains through technology. The authors argue that inefficient delivery can frustrate business clients and cost firms future work.
qs: According to Becker et al. (2003), ‘client loyalty is decreasing as companies increasingly base purchases of legal services on a more objective assessment of their value, defined as benefits net of price.’
According to Khandelwal and Gottschalk (2003) law firms are increasingly being pressured by their clients to achieve productivity gains through the use of technology to become more efficient.

kp.k: Hourly billing can undermine incentives for efficiency
kp.d: The authors identify a conflict between reducing task time and generating hourly revenue. Following Kay and Dublin, they argue that efficiency may not financially benefit firms without changed billing structures. They also report that lawyers can be penalised when knowledge-sharing activity reduces billable hours; the paper does not quantify this effect or specify a replacement pricing model.
qs: However, if billing structures are not changed, the efficiencies obtained through KM may not benefit a firm financially (Kay, 2003, p.1).
In certain cases, Dublin (2005) notes that lawyers may be penalised for their efforts at knowledge transfer, if it has the effect of reducing their billable hours.

kp.k: Individual practices and reputation discourage collective knowledge sharing
kp.d: The paper argues that client-focused individual practices, income tied to time spent and clients' preference for particular lawyers weaken incentives to share expertise. Reporting Terrett, it notes that clients may pay premiums for star lawyers rather than select solely on firm credentials.
qs: One of the major obstacles in implementing KM practices in law firms is that there exist few financial incentives for lawyers to share knowledge with their colleagues.
Therefore, lawyers are not typically recognised for adopting a team-based approach to legal work nor are they rewarded for sharing their expertise.

kp.k: Time demands and technological resistance impede implementation
kp.d: The authors identify lawyers' limited time for documenting knowledge and resistance to unfamiliar technology as barriers. Citing Dublin and Terrett, they argue that successful traditional practices can make change difficult and that systems demanding substantial manual input are unlikely to succeed.
qs: Therefore, systems that require a great deal of time spent inputting information have little chance of success in most law firms (Dublin, 2005).
It is difficult to introduce new modes of thinking into a firm that is currently successful and that has been successful for a long period of time using traditional practices.
Time spent sharing knowledge and experience is time not spent billing clients (Terrett, 1998, p.75).

kp.k: Retirement and turnover threaten retained expertise
kp.d: The authors anticipate loss of experienced lawyers' tacit knowledge as senior lawyers retire, recommending transfer to younger lawyers before departure. They also argue that repetitive work and insufficient learning can contribute to turnover, reducing the firm's knowledge assets. These are qualitative claims without retirement or turnover estimates.
qs: Due to the increasing number of senior lawyers that are approaching the age of retirement, valuable information will be lost if their experience and expertise is improperly documented.
It is therefore highly desirable to transfer the knowledge and wisdom of older lawyers to younger lawyers (Dublin, 2005).

In addition, providing professional satisfaction to employees is essential because employees who are not learning and those who are engaged in repetitive tasks will get bored, grow disillusioned and eventually leave the firm (Terrett, 1998, p.72).

kp.k: Global competition heightens knowledge and recruitment pressures
kp.d: Reporting Becker and colleagues, the paper describes global companies seeking legal support across their business locations. It also reports Dublin's argument that younger lawyers expect modern information technology, linking knowledge-transfer capabilities to graduate recruitment and competition for expertise.
qs: According to Becker et al. (2003), global companies increasingly seek out law firms that provide continuous support for all business locations.

It is therefore increasingly important that firms remain on top of the latest information technologies in order to facilitate knowledge transfer and thereby recruit the best graduates, who have come to expect such capabilities in a modern law firm.

kp.k: Trust and human contact underpin knowledge transfer
kp.d: The authors distinguish interpersonal, knowledge-based trust from trust in the institution and its safeguards. Drawing on Bender and Fish, they recommend human contact beyond computer-mediated interaction to build relationships and willingness to share. Senior management support is presented as essential to establishing a sharing culture.
qs: Thus, in addition to establishing a supportive culture, it is also imperative for the organization to develop trust and loyalty among firm members.
In order to build trust, a company needs to ensure there is adequate human contact between employees.

In order to build personal relationships and networks while also building trust, an environment must go beyond interaction which is facilitated solely through the use of computers (Bender and Fish, 2000).

kp.k: Communities of practice and mentoring support professional learning
kp.d: The paper recommends communities of practice for ongoing collaboration around shared problems and expertise, alongside mentoring in which senior employees develop junior colleagues. It cites HP and Xerox as examples of communities of practice and Ernst & Young as an example of linking mentoring participation to appraisal and rewards; these are reported cross-industry examples, not new law-firm findings.
qs: People within COP deepen their knowledge and expertise by interacting on an ongoing basis.
One program the HR department can institute is a mentoring program in which senior employees are expected to help with the learning and development of junior colleagues.
To ensure the success of the program, participation can be tied to appraisal and reward systems, demonstrated by the successful implementation of such a system by Ernst & Young (Dunford, 2000).

kp.k: Human resources should reward collective knowledge contributions
kp.d: The authors assign HR responsibility for supporting knowledge-sharing culture and designing incentives. They recommend social and non-monetary rewards, recognition of group effort and pay-for-knowledge that compensates sharing. They also recommend continuous review of reward-system effectiveness rather than assuming implementation alone produces results.
qs: Bollinger and Smith (2001) observe that reward systems must attempt to reward group effort and not just individual effort, to ensure people will work collectively.
The organization also needs to create a pay-for-knowledge system that emphasises the sharing of knowledge and pays people for sharing.
Once the reward system has been implemented, the firm needs to ensure it is successful, which can be determined by applying a continuous review system (Arora, 2002, p.254).

kp.k: Knowledge leadership must maintain useful technological resources
kp.d: The paper describes intranets, databases, portals, groupware, email, teleconferencing and West KM as tools for access and collaboration. It recommends a Chief Knowledge Officer and implementation team, with the CKO and HR responsible for relevant, non-repetitive content. These are KM technologies and governance recommendations, not claims about generative AI.
qs: Another program being implemented is West KM, software designed to interconnect all the documents and information within a business.
The CKO and the HR department will be in charge of ensuring that these databases and portals are full of relevant and important but non-repetitive information.
Firms must create a Chief Knowledge Officer and a KM implementation team

kp.k: Proposed benefits include service quality, integration and risk reduction
kp.d: Drawing on Stuart Kay (2003), the paper lists potential benefits including faster document production, access to specialist expertise, reduced stress, retention of departing lawyers' knowledge and easier integration of new lawyers. It also suggests that effective knowledge transfer may help avoid professional negligence suits. These benefits are presented without quantified outcome evidence, and the paper acknowledges difficulties measuring financial returns.
qs: Effective KM can assist in the integration of new lawyers into the firm.
Effective transfer of knowledge may help avoid professional negligence suits.
In many firms, KM capabilities and benefits are not properly measured because the metrics required to measure the financial returns are not readily available.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: No explicit AI-related claim or prediction is made in this source.
pts.d: Kabene, King and Skaini examine knowledge management (KM), human resources and conventional information technology in law firms, rather than artificial intelligence. They claim that successful KM can improve efficiency, knowledge retention, client service and competitive advantage. These are KM claims, not claims about AI, and the references to data mining, process automation and document-search software do not establish an AI-specific argument.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.d: The paper synthesises published KM literature, cited law-firm studies and organisational examples. It does not report AI performance tests, AI adoption outcomes or AI-related legal-service cases. Its discussion of West KM concerns document interconnection and database searching, not an identified AI capability or measured AI outcome.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI adoption or impact timeframe is specified; the conditions concern KM implementation in the paper's 2006 context.
pts.d: The authors condition the benefits of KM on organisational culture, structure, incentives, management support and human interaction. These qualifications should not be recast as forecasts about AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source identifies stakeholders affected by KM, but makes no AI-specific claims about any group.
pts.d: The KM discussion concerns law firms, lawyers, junior and retiring senior colleagues, HR professionals, knowledge officers and clients. The authors assign HR responsibility for sharing incentives and mentoring, and assign HR and the chief knowledge officer responsibility for repository content. These are organisational KM responsibilities, not predicted AI-driven changes in employment or legal-service provision.
